edits.old: MongoDB's multi-region guide documents node placements and tradeoffs for three-region 2+2+1 and 1+1+1 designs, and a two-region 2+3 option for organizations limited to two regions. It says the five-node, two-region design can remain read-only if the majority region fails until an administrator reconfigures nodes; the three-node design is less expensive but can have latency during planned maintenance and when clients continue serving requests from the original primary region. (medium confidence)

evidence.quote: If your company is limited to only 2 regions, you can use a variation on the 5-Node, 3-Region  architecture, in which you have 5 nodes distributed between two regions.
If the majority region is lost, the system will still remain available in read-only mode until a majority of nodes are brought into an electable state.
To restore the functional cluster, an administrator needs to reconfigure the 2 read-only nodes to electable nodes.
you can leverage a less expensive architecture by using 1 node in each of 3 regions.
if your app tier in the original primary region is still servicing user requests, there will be increased latency as requests are routed across multiple regions.
We do not generally recommend this configuration because regular, planned maintenance of Atlas nodes will cause temporary latency spikes.
The following diagram shows 2 examples of a 2+2+1 topology, which is discussed in detail below.

statements.statement: Guide documents 2+2+1 and 1+1+1 three-region designs and a 2+3 two-region option for organizations limited to two regions.
The 2+3 design can remain read-only if the majority region fails until an administrator reconfigures nodes.
The three-node design is less expensive but has latency during planned maintenance and when clients keep using the original primary region.

edits.rationale: The Atlas multi-region deployment paradigm guide documents the 2+2+1, 2+3 and 1+1+1 designs and the stated tradeoffs. The claim's cited billing page does not cover them, but the guide does.
